claims.text: Melt-spinning Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 at cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s produces an amorphous ribbon.
A brief isothermal anneal at 900–1000 K immediately after melt-spinning is a sub-crystallization treatment for this alloy.
Post-quench sub-crystallization annealing will promote atomic-scale structural relaxation.
The proposed structural relaxation will reduce internal stresses in the melt-spun alloy.
The proposed structural relaxation will reduce the density of embryonic crystalline clusters.
The regions targeted by relaxation are particularly prone to phosphorus-driven eutectic or non-eutectic primary crystallization.
Localized rearrangement during annealing will place the amorphous alloy in a lower-energy metastable configuration.
Reducing structural heterogeneities will reduce the number of nucleation sites active during subsequent heating.
The proposed anneal will postpone or suppress primary crystallization during reheating.
Annealed ribbons will retain a more homogeneous amorphous structure than directly as-quenched ribbons.
Annealing will raise the crystallization onset temperature during reheating by tens of kelvin.
Annealing will produce fewer and less pronounced exothermic peaks associated with primary crystallization.
Slow cooling of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 produces a complex multiphase crystalline microstructure.
Accelerated cooling produces fewer crystalline phases than slow cooling.
Reported transformations in this alloy include FCC A and orthorhombic E crystallization.
The cited study identifies a rapid-cooling DSC crystallization boundary typically below 1000 K.
A hold at 900–1000 K can be made long enough for relaxation but short enough to avoid initiating crystallization.
Phosphorus and high mixing entropy promote glass formation in this alloy under extremely rapid cooling.

contradictions.description: The proposed range includes 1000 K, while the boundary requires the hold to remain below 1000 K; the endpoint therefore does not satisfy the stated boundary.

The prediction only specifies an increase of 'tens of Kelvin,' whereas the falsification rule demands an increase greater than 50 K. A smaller shift within the predicted range could therefore be treated as a failure by the stated test.
